title: Vayechi: not in God's place (Genesis 50:15–21)
hook: Joseph refuses revenge: "ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vayechi: twelve sons, twelve different blessings. Your line was each one his own blessing. Did you tell two people what you see in them? Today, Jacob is buried, and the brothers are suddenly afraid. Day two hundred twenty.

There's a particular fear that shows up after a funeral. The parent who held everyone together is gone, and suddenly old debts look different. Was my brother only being nice because Dad was watching? Joseph's brothers feel exactly that. For seventeen years in Egypt, Joseph has fed them and protected them. But now their father is buried. And they think: maybe he was just waiting. Maybe now he'll pay us back for the pit and the sale. So they send him a message. Today: what Joseph does with the power to punish.
screen: `AFTER THE FUNERAL.` → `MAYBE HE WAS JUST WAITING.` → `THE POWER TO PUNISH.`

segments.voice: The brothers' message says: before he died, your father told us to tell you, please forgive your brothers. The Torah never shows Jacob saying any such thing. The Talmud concludes they made it up, and draws a surprising rule from it: you may soften the truth for the sake of peace. Joseph hears their words, and he cries. Then the brothers come and throw themselves down: we're your slaves. Remember the dreams? The sheaves bowing, the stars bowing? Here it is, finally. The brothers on the ground, offering themselves. Joseph could take it. Instead he says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Fear not; for am I in the place of God?" In Hebrew, ha-tachat Elohim ani. Am I standing where God stands? Judging and punishing isn't my seat. And then: "ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good." Notice he doesn't pretend. He says it plainly: you meant evil. What they did was wrong, and he names it. But he refuses to make himself the one who settles the account. He says he'll provide for them and their little ones, and the text says he comforted them and spoke to their hearts. And with that, the book of Genesis ends. Joseph dies at a hundred and ten, still in Egypt. When a congregation finishes reading a book of the Torah, everyone stands and calls out: chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another.
screen: `A MESSAGE FATHER NEVER SENT.` · `THE BROTHERS ON THE GROUND.` · `AM I IN THE PLACE OF GOD?` · `YOU MEANT EVIL. HE MEANT GOOD.` · then, large: `NOT MY PLACE TO PUNISH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: decline one chance for revenge. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has wronged you, and a way you could get even, even a small one. The pointed comment, the cold shoulder, the story you could tell about them. Name the wrong honestly, like Joseph: they did that, it was wrong. Then imagine setting the payback down, because it isn't your seat. Just for today. The bell holds the time.
Vayechi. The last portion of Genesis, which ends with Joseph refusing revenge: am I in the place of God?
Your line: not my place to punish. Today, when a chance to get even shows up, name the wrong if you need to, and let the payback go. Day two hundred twenty.

screen: `DAY 220 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SHEMOT: THESE ARE THE NAMES.`

howItsDone: When the reading of a whole book of the Torah is completed in synagogue, the congregation stands and says chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek; Jewish law also forbids taking revenge or bearing a grudge, from Leviticus 19:18.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. your father is buried. the brothers who sold you are lying at your feet, offering to be your slaves. what do you do?
options: accept; your dreams have come true.
tell them it's not your place to punish, and provide for them.
forgive them, but send them away.
fork.reveal: Joseph said: fear not, am I in the place of God? you meant evil, God meant it for good. then he promised to feed them and their children, and comforted them.

original.note: Hebrew: am I in the place of God? Joseph's answer to his brothers (Genesis 50:19).

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph forgave and forgot.
what it means: Joseph names the wrong and still refuses to be the one who punishes.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud learns from the brothers' invented message that one may alter the truth for the sake of peace (Yevamot 65b).
